overview: These map entries cover ducal Florence and the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, rather than the earlier Florentine republic. Medici rulers combined government, collecting and scientific patronage; later Lorraine rulers introduced important reforms. Livorno’s merchants, hospital children and village families left different kinds of evidence from the grand dukes’ palaces.

periods.title: Ducal Florence
periods.summary: The map begins around 1530. Cosimo I became duke in 1537 and received the grand-ducal title in 1569.

periods.title: Medici grand dukes
periods.summary: The Medici grand duchy outlasted the atlas’s change from Florence to Tuscany at 1650. The dynasty’s rule ended with Gian Gastone’s death in 1737.

periods.title: Lorraine rule and French interruption
periods.summary: Lorraine rule followed the Medici. French administration introduced civil registration in 1808; the restored Lorraine government reorganized it after 1814. Tuscany joined the Italian unification process in 1860.

items.text: Cosimo I sponsored botanical gardens at Pisa in 1544 and Florence in 1545. Growing and comparing plants became part of organized study. A garden could be a research collection as well as a pleasant place to walk; the grand duke also supported mapmaking and mathematical instruments.

The Uffizi began in 1560 as a government building. Thirteen magistracies were brought together, while workshops made precious objects for the court. The famous art museum’s name means “offices”: its early inhabitants had paperwork as well as paintings to think about.

The Accademia del Cimento worked at the Medici court from 1657 to 1667. Its members investigated temperature, air pressure and other physical questions through experiments. Court sponsorship gave them instruments and space, but this small learned circle was not a school open to every Tuscan child.

Twelve surviving Florentine thermometers, made in the mid-seventeenth century, stand in a wooden rack. Their liquid was alcohol; black enamel dots marked single degrees and white dots tens. Comparable instruments let observers compare indoor and outdoor conditions. These were fifty-degree scales, not today’s Celsius scale.

Anna Maria Luisa de’ Medici’s 1737 family pact helped keep the dynasty’s artistic collections in Florence after its rule ended. Under the Lorraine government, the Uffizi opened to the public in 1769. Dynastic change could therefore alter who saw a collection without sending all its pictures away.

Pietro Leopoldo’s criminal reform abolished the death penalty in 1786 and argued that punishment should allow the offender to become a useful member of society. This was a major reform, not an irreversible ending: capital punishment was partly restored four years later.

Florence’s Innocenti hospital had cared for abandoned children since the fifteenth century and continued under grand-ducal government. Babies were placed with wet nurses; older children could live with rural foster families. Its records reveal a network of paid care extending far beyond the elegant hospital façade.

Some parents left identifying tokens with a baby: a coin, button, medal or piece of ribbon, sometimes divided so matching halves could be recognized. The objects show hopes of identifying children later; they do not tell us that every separation ended in a reunion.

The Innocenti token collection needs careful dating. Most surviving objects belong to 1827 to 1921, so many are later than the grand duchy. Rarer late-seventeenth-century examples survive with baptism files, while earlier registers often describe tokens whose physical objects are now missing.

The Livorno laws of 1591 and 1593 offered privileges to attract merchants. The invitation included households, not just lone traders. Bringing people to a port meant finding homes and sustaining communities as well as moving cargo; privileges depended on particular laws and groups.

A short sample from the 1593 Livornina reads “abitare con le uostre famiglie”: “live with your families.” The transcription preserves the historical Italian spelling uostre, with u where modern Italian uses v. These Latin-letter words let us hear official policy speak directly about household migration.

Livorno’s Jewish community could maintain worship, own property, pursue study and print Hebrew books under its privileges. Its quarter was open rather than a compulsory enclosed ghetto. This particular arrangement should not be treated as evidence that all religious groups everywhere in Tuscany enjoyed equal rights.

Village births and marriages eventually generated paperwork in Florence. Examples include an Arcidosso marriage register from 1819 and a Marciano birth record from 1843. Parishes and local officials sent extracts and duplicates to the central civil-registration office: ordinary family events became part of a state archive.

ending.text: The grand duchy did not survive until the map label’s 1878 endpoint. Tuscany entered the unifying Italian state in 1860. Its communities continued, while regional civil-registration records were eventually transferred to the Florence State Archive.
